data.title: Adex Mining Announces Adjournment of Appeal Before New Brunswick Energy and Utilities Board
data.description:
Toronto, Ontario--(Newsfile Corp. - November 6, 2026) - Adex Mining Inc.  ("Adex" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that Adex Minerals Corp. ("Adex Minerals"), the Company's wholly-owned subsidiary through which Adex holds its interest in the Mount Pleasant mining project in New Brunswick, has agreed jointly with the Mining Recorder, Resource and Development Branch of the New Brunswick Department of Natural Resources and Energy (the "Mining Recorder") to adjourn the Appeal (as defined below) previously announced by Adex and originally scheduled to proceed before the New Brunswick Energy and Utilities Board (the "NBEUB") on December 3 and 4, 2026. The formal hearing is now scheduled to take place on March 11 and 12, 2027. The decision to adjourn the Appeal was made jointly and by mutual consent with counsel for the Mining Recorder. The adjournment will allow the Company to focus its efforts and internal resources on achieving a successful outcome to its ongoing strategic review process through including identifying and executing a value-maximizing transaction for Adex in respect of the Mount Pleasant project.

As previously disclosed in its press releases dated July 29, 2026 and September 10, 2026, Adex Minerals received correspondence dated July 13, 2026 from the Mining Recorder advising that the mineral claim 1505 (the "Mineral Claim" upon which the Mount Pleasant project is situated) had been cancelled by the Mining Recorder and placed in protected status due to failures by Adex Minerals to complete sufficient work program expenditures as required under s. 11(1) of the General Regulation - Mining Act, N.B. Reg. 86-98. Adex Minerals appealed this decision on July 29, 2026 (the "Appeal"). On September 9, 2026, after an interim stay hearing conducted before the NBEUB on August 31, 2026, Adex Minerals successfully obtained an interim stay of the Mining Recorder's cancellation of the Mineral Claim, and the Mineral Claim was reinstated in the name of Adex Minerals pending a final determination of the Appeal. This status remains in effect pending the newly-rescheduled Appeal hearing.

The adjournment does not reflect any concession on the part of the Company, and the Company remains confident in its position on, and is optimistic of a favourable result in, the hearing of the Appeal. Adex Minerals continues to believe that the Mining Recorder failed to engage with Adex Minerals' good faith proposals to complete the necessary expenditures in a timely manner and acted unreasonably in imposing arbitrary deadlines after eschewing Adex Minerals' good faith efforts to comply. Adex's special committee of independent directors continues to work with its external advisors and remains fully engaged in pursuing potential transaction opportunities with interested parties in accordance with its ongoing mandate previously described by the Company.

ABOUT ADEX

Adex Mining Inc. is a Canadian junior mining company with an experienced management team. The Company has maintained stewardship over the Mount Pleasant property while evaluating strategic alternatives. The Mount Pleasant property is a multi-metal project that is host to promising tungsten-molybdenum and tin-indium-zinc mineralization. The common shares of Adex trade on the TSX Venture Exchange under the stock symbol "ADE".

data.title: IPOs Struggle in Tech Selloff. Berkshire Has a Winner. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Bary

The old investment adage to avoid initial public offerings has held up this year, as many stocks are trading well below their IPO prices.

Barron's looked at 18 companies that made their U.S. stock-market debuts in 2026, including marquee offerings like SpaceX, Cerebras Systems, Innio, Madison Air Solutions and Jersey Mike's, found that 15 of them are below their offering prices. Many are down 50% or more.

SK Hynix, already public in South Korea, made its U.S. debut in July through an offering of American depositary shares. That stock also is trading below its U.S. offering price in July.

Why do IPOs often falter? Companies that come public often are in hot industries, and carry high valuations to reflect investor optimism. That enthusiasm often wanes, however. This year, some deals were keyed off the AI buildout and enthusiasm for that trend has faded.

There are some winners, notably Arxis, a defense contractor with an aerospace focus; Pershing Square, Bill Ackman's investment management company, and Bending Spoons, the rollup of mature tech companies like AOL.

Give Berkshire Hathaway some credit. The company headed now by CEO Greg Abel picked the right deal when it invested $600 million in Bending Spoons at the July IPO at $29 a share. The stock traded recently at $45, up 55%. In October, Berkshire bought another $330 million of stock at $33.

Berkshire rarely buys IPOs — reflecting former CEO Warren Buffett's well-founded aversion to them. It participated in Snowflake's IPO in 2020.

Looking at some of the larger deals, SpaceX trades around $131, against an IPO price of $135; Cerebras at $82, less than half its IPO price of $185; and SK Hynix at $124, versus its U.S. offering price of $149.

One of the better ways to play IPOs in a diversified way is through the Renaissance IPO ETF. It adds newly public companies every three months as part of a regular rebalancing and companies cycle out after three years. Individual holdings are capped at a 10% weighting at rebalancing.

Its largest holdings now are SpaceX at nearly 10%, followed by SK Hynix and Astera Labs, both at more than 7%. The ETF, now around $45, is off about 2% so far this year.

Be careful about SK Hynix ADRs. While chip stocks have come under pressure, SK Hynix's U.S. shares trade at a big premium to the Korean shares that Barron's estimates is close to 50%.

Busted IPOs also can be a good place to look for values, and there are many companies to comb through this year.

Write to Andrew Bary at andrew.bary@barrons.com

data.title: Canadian dollar posts steepest decline since January on surprise jobs loss
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

The Canadian dollar fell by the most in nine months against its US counterpart on Friday after domestic data showed the economy shed jobs for a third straight month, cooling expectations for Bank of Canada interest rate hikes.

The loonie was trading 0.8% lower at 1.4128 per US dollar, or 70.78 US cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since October 19 at 1.4137. It was the steepest daily decline for the currency since January 30.

  • For the week, the currency was down 1.1%, after three straight weeks of gains, as equity markets globally were buffeted by a selloff in AI stocks.

  • "The CAD has failed to deliver on the potential for its recent rebound to extend this week," Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, FX strategists at Scotiabank, said in a note.

  • "Elevated equity-market volatility has overshadowed pretty much everything else, although the combination of weak Canadian and strong US jobs data has given the CAD an added nudge lower into the weekend," the strategists said.

  • Canadian employment fell 4,700 in October and the jobless rate rose to a six-month high of 6.7%. Analysts had expected a 13,600 jobs gain.

  • Chances the Bank of Canada would tighten in December dipped to 36% from 40%, swap market data showed.

  • The Canadian central bank unveiled on Thursday a new five-year monetary policy framework with the federal finance ministry, keeping its inflation target unchanged at 2%.

  • Also on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney's budget showed that he plans to use windfall oil revenue to boost Canada's productivity and build infrastructure while keeping his previous fiscal goals intact.

  • US nonfarm payrolls increased more than expected in October, boosting the US dollar against a basket of major currencies.

  • US crude futures CLc1 posted a steep weekly decline after the election losses of US President Donald Trump's Republican Party raised hopes of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran. Oil is one of Canada's major exports.

  • The Canadian 2-year yield (CA2YT=RR) was down one basis points at 3.146%, while it fell 4.5 basis points further below the equivalent US rate to a gap of about 137 basis points.

data.title: U.S. Stocks Mixed After Jobs Data, Muted AI Rebound — Update
data.description:
By Rob Curran

U.S. stocks were mixed as strong jobs data and a modest rebound for artificial-intelligence companies failed to quell investor nerves about the sustainability of the AI boom.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to 51285.73. Meanwhile, the broad S&P 500 gained 23.13 points, or 0.31%, to 7376.86. The S&P 500 had its biggest weekly loss since the tariff scare in April 2025. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 264.43 points, or 1.09%, to 24579.42. The Nasdaq's gains waned slightly near the closing bell, suggesting traders remained on edge going into the weekend.

U.S. employers added 165,000 workers to payrolls in October, thumping economists' expectations of a 59,000 addition.

Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar gained after the jobs data on increased expectations of more Federal Reserve rate hikes.

The yield on the policy-sensitive two-year Treasury rose 0.045 percentage point to 4.520%. Still, the two-year yield has now fallen for six straight weeks, incurring the biggest six-week loss in more than a year. The 10-year Treasury note added 0.023 percentage point to 4.858%. The yield on the 30-year bond rose 0.010 percentage point to 5.26%. The 30-year yield has fallen for five straight weeks, the longest losing streak since 2022.

Oil futures were more or less flat, rising 31 cents, or 0.3%, to $90.83 a barrel in New York as traders awaited changes in Iran policy in the wake of the midterm elections. Oil prices had their biggest weekly retreat since April as comments from President Trump and Vice President Vance suggested the U.S. may seek an exit from the conflict.

Gold futures, which gained during Thursday's stock-market rout, gave back some of those gains falling $38, or 0.9%, to $4064.50 a troy ounce.

"Democratic control of Congress is gold-supportive, as Democrats tend to be associated with greater government spending and wider deficits," said James Steel, chief precious metals analyst at brokerage HSBC Global Investment Research, in a note to clients. Another reason gold crossed back above the psychologically significant $4,000-per-ounce level may be optimism about an end to the Middle East war, he said. "If the Democratic sweep brings the possibility of a settlement with Iran closer, then perhaps the argument for higher rates may be diluted. This backdrop would aid gold."

Overnight, Japan's Nikkei 225 entered bear-market territory. The Kospi index in South Korea, a proxy for AI sentiment due to high profile companies like SK hynix and Samsung Electronics, fell 6% and is now down 44% from its June peak.

In the U.S., the PHLX "SOX" Semiconductor sector index rose 4.2%, recouping some of the 12% loss on Thursday.

Among the hardest hit chip makers Nvidia rose 2.8% to $186.64. Cloud-computing firm CoreWeave added 6.3% to $46.40.

Three major investors who plan to participate in Anthropic's initial-public offering said the valuation will likely need to come down from its current level at $1.5 trillion, with one saying it could be closer to $1 trillion.

Tesla recouped some of its postelection losses after shares rose 4.2% to $358.22. Chief Executive Elon Musk said the company would wind down production of its Cybertruck electric pickup at its gigafactory in Texas next year.

Meanwhile, Alphabet, Google's parent, plans to open a Texas factory to produce its Wing brand of drones.

The increase in Treasury yields muted the lift in consumer-facing industries from the jobs data.

Shares of Charter Communications slid 6.2% to $118.07 after the broadband provider logged another quarterly decline in internet and video subscribers, extending a longstanding trend in the industry.

Humana shares rose 5.3% to $433.74 after the health insurer raised its projection for 2026 earnings, having paid out slightly less of its premium revenue on medical expenses in the latest quarter.

Moderna swung to a third-quarter profit and raised its full-year revenue growth forecast as Covid-19 vaccine demand steadied after a long slide.

Write to Rob Curran at rob.curran@wsj.com

data.title: In Republican collapse, Colorado military town elects Democrat for the first time
data.description:
Key points:
  • Army vet Killin becomes first Democrat to win district created in 1970
  • Unaffiliated voters swell to 53% of El Paso County electorate, county data shows
  • Killin outraised her Republican opponent

By Andrew Hay and Brad Brooks

Colorado Springs, a military town and global center for Christian evangelism, has sent a Republican to Washington every election since its US House of Representatives district was created in 1970.

Then came 2026.

The victory of Jessica Killin, an Army veteran who was among dozens of Democrats who flipped a seat this week, is one of the starkest examples of how the party built its resounding win on affordability issues, demographics and candidates, one district at a time.

In an area with five military installations, where soldiers pack fast-food restaurants at lunchtime, Killin's triumph relied on votes of veterans, service members and their families, who represent about a third of the population, and for whom the war in Iran is personal. A soldier deployed from the city's Fort Carson US Army base was among the first Americans to die in the conflict.

Killin, a first-time candidate, said her win was a repudiation of Republican incumbent Jeff Crank's support for President Donald Trump and underscored voters' frustrations with the Iran war, tariffs and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

A supporter who canvassed for her found immigration also was on the minds of Latinos in a district where the population of metropolitan Colorado Springs more than doubled to around 782,000 in the last four decades, bringing greater ethnic diversity and a younger, more highly educated electorate.

"I am resolved to make the history that really matters, combating horrific corruption and chaos that we are all honestly sick of in Washington, DC," Killin, a former US Army paratrooper and aide to ex-second gentleman Doug Emhoff, told reporters on Thursday.

Crank had tried to portray Killin as an outsider.

"We cannot let our community turn into Denver or Boulder," Crank posted on social media last week, referring to the two Democratic-controlled cities to the north.

Killin targeted centrist and left-leaning residents in the state’s second-largest city, and her hometown, who in the past three presidential cycles abandoned both major parties, swelling unaffiliated voters by nearly half to 53% of the electorate in El Paso County, according to county data.

In a metropolitan area where more than 200 space, aerospace, cybersecurity, and defense companies employ around 111,000 people, and account for over 40% of the local economy, Killin hammered Crank's support of Trump's "reckless" war in Iran and argued that Congress needed to reclaim its war-powers authority.

Karl Schneider, 57, a former US special forces officer and ex-vice chairman of the El Paso Republican Party, backed Killin to rein in a presidency he sees as militarily out of control.

"Donald Trump is a clear and present danger to the United States of America, our republic, and I think to the rest of the world," said Schneider, an executive at an AI cybersecurity advisory firm who served as a US Army Green Beret.

For Republican voter Rick Wood, 67, Crank failed to help tackle high gas and grocery prices and tied himself too closely to Trump, whose approval rating is near a career low of 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos national poll.

"They ran on Trump's coattails," said Wood, a US Air Force veteran.

'NEVER SEEN BEFORE'

Some Republicans interviewed by Reuters in the district that is home to the Focus on the Family evangelical organization were stunned by the blue wave, saying they feared the country would descend into communism, echoing warnings from Trump about the recent rise of left-wing Democratic candidates.

Politics professor Sara Hagedorn saw Killin, and other Democrats who won in former Republican strongholds, as a possible return to the fiscally responsible "Blue Dog" Democrats of the 1990s and early 2000s who worked across party lines.

"She has a real opportunity here to be a real moderate or independent voice within the Democratic Party," said Hagedorn, who teaches at the University of Colorado, Colorado Springs.

Killin's campaign coffers swelled after the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee listed the district as "in play" in February, the first time the committee had targeted the area.

Bruce Barron, 65, a former Republican congressional aide, canvassed for Killin in southeast Colorado Springs where the school district has around 54% Hispanic students and many of the Black community live.

"Every Hispanic I talked to, it resonates with them, the concern about Hispanics not being safe under the Trump administration,” said Barron.

Killin’s campaign outraised Crank’s by nearly two to one with $5.6 million in funds. Crank received $5.8 million in outside spending, giving the two similar war chests.

Killin deployed over 400 volunteers to knock on over 100,000 doors while hosting around 150 events to meet voters, according to her campaign.

As Kyle Ries, 40, canvassed for Killin in south Colorado Springs, where American flags fly outside many homes and fuel-hungry pickups stand in driveways, he met conservatives willing to support Killin after they saw Crank back a war that has stoked energy prices.

"This is a candidate that this district has never seen before," Ries, an IT professional, said of Killin.

data.title: Google Exec Leaves SpaceX Board — WSJ
data.description:
By Becky Peterson

Don Harrison, a Google executive and longtime SpaceX director, has stepped down from the role on the rocketmaker's board of directors. SpaceX said his departure, announced Friday, was effective immediately.

Harrison, the president of global partnerships and corporate development at Google, joined the SpaceX board in 2015, overseeing an investment that grew to $75.2 billion by the end of the third quarter.

His departure comes as the SpaceX board weighs a possible merger with Chief Executive Elon Musk's electric-vehicle maker Tesla. Both companies faced selloffs this week following the mid-term elections.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: TSX posts weekly gain as metal mining shares rally
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

Canada's main stock index rose on Friday, led by technology and metal mining shares, as investors weighed downbeat domestic jobs data that could reduce prospects of further tightening from the Bank of Canada.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index ended up 183.82 points, or 0.5%, at 35,789.09, after posting on Thursday its steepest drop in five months. For the week, the index was up 0.5%, after two straight weekly declines.

  • Huge Democrat gains in the US midterm elections this week led to investors anticipating increased scrutiny of the AI industry, triggering volatility in technology stocks and safe-haven demand for US Treasuries.

  • "What we saw post midterms was US Treasury yields came down, the US dollar weakened. That helped gold rebound," said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. "It was a great week for mining."

  • The materials sector , which includes metal mining shares, rose 2.6%, lifting its weekly advance to 11.4%.

  • Canadian employment fell 4,700 in October and the jobless rate rose to a six-month high of 6.7%. It was the first jobs report since the Bank of Canada's recent move to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.

  • "It's a sign that the Canadian economy is not going gangbusters," Cieszynski said. "It's muddling along at best and so they're probably not under as much pressure to raise rates again."

  • Technology rose 1.8% as US tech stocks rebounded.

  • Energy added 0.2%. US crude oil futures settled 0.3% higher at $90.83 a barrel but were still posting a sharp weekly decline as investors weighed prospects of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

  • Industrials (.GSPTTIN) were a drag, falling 0.9%, and heavily weighted financials ended 0.2% lower.

  • Shares of Trisura Group tumbled 29.9% after the specialty insurer's quarterly results missed estimates.
